common_name: Eleanor's Pride Bearded Iris (1961 Dykes Medal Powder Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Eleanor's Pride is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Eleanor's Pride, hybridized by Edward Watkins from 'Jane Phillips' crossed with 'Blue Rhythm' and registered in 1952, produces large, broad, ruffled standards and falls in a rich powder-blue self with a light lemon-yellow beard. A mature clump produces a distinctive tricolor display over the course of a bloom cycle: medium-blue buds opening to lighter blue fresh flowers that fade to nearly pure white by their second day. It earned the Award of Merit in 1958 and the American Dykes Medal in 1961, cementing its place among the most influential blue bearded irises of its era. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the old woody center.

common_name: Charlie's Ginny Louisiana Iris (Bright Rose Bitone Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Hybridized by Louisiana iris breeder Charles W. Arny Jr. from 'Louise Arny' crossed with a cross of 'W. B. MacMillan' and 'Tressie Cook', and registered in 1972, Charlie's Ginny bears bright rose bitone flowers with contrasting yellow styles on stalks reaching about 42 inches, blooming midseason. It earned an Honorable Mention from the American Iris Society in 1976 and went on to become an influential breeding parent in its own right, passed down into later bitone-breeding Louisiana iris lines including 'Helen Naish' and 'Fiesta Gal'. Keep it in full sun with reliably moist to wet soil through the bloom period, and divide crowded clumps after flowering to maintain vigor.
